This is one of those topics that has been completely ruined by the omission of context.

The original quote has been presented as "We are developers, not gamers." That's what gets people riled up. The important statement that was made within seconds of the first that helps to establish context is, "There is not some sort of unwritten law that unless you call yourself a gamer you can’t love video games."

So all the people arguing that being a gamer is the same as being someone who plays video games are already completely outside the scope of the issue. Rami didn't say that you can be a developer without enjoying games. He specifically said you can enjoy games without identifying as a gamer.

So that leads us to the next stage in this mess. All of a sudden a group of people now needs to find a reason to find fault with the delineation between gamer and person who plays and enjoys video games. I've seen terms like elitist thrown around, and really awful analogy of people who don't like movies making movies. All pointless arguments because they're struggling around the simple issue of what delineates a gamer from someone who plays and enjoys videogames.

With every hobby, there are people whose involvement is relatively casual, and those whose involvement is quite deep. It's the difference between the person who plays and very much enjoys Pokemon, and the person who plays it, enjoys it, has a wall in their home dedicated to pokemon posters, collects Pokemon figurines, visits Pokemon discussion forums daily, follows the development on the latest Pokemon titles, and is first in line the night before the premier of "Pokemon, Mon - The Rastafarian Pokemon Cinematic Spectacular!"

There's no good or bad. There's no implied judgement. For one person it's a hobby that starts when they load up the game and ends when they turn it off. For others, it's closer to a way of life.

This kind of distinction is made for pretty much every hobby. In global terms, it's the difference between a participant and an enthusiast. Again, theer is no judgement in delineating the two. There is a difference, after all.

So are we accurate to compare the delineation between gamers and people who enjoy games to someone who doesn't like movies but tries to make them in an attempt to discredit the distinction? No. As this article points out, Orson Welles would have something to say about the varacity of that statement. But more importantly, the statement that parallels the gamer version would more accurately be, "You don't have to be a cinephile to make good movies."

Anyone who has ever watched Mythbusters even semi-regularly knows that Adam Savage is a self-identified cinephile. He's got an impressive collection of memorabilia from some of his favorite movies, including costumes, props, and all kinds of other goodies. He knows his favorite movies inside and out.

Do you need to be a cinephile to be able to make movies? Nope. You don't. You can watch movies, enjoy movies, learn a lot from movies without being a cinephile.
